accepted_impacts.label: Filtered database tree results for overloaded objects
accepted_impacts.llm_reason: When loading filtered tree contents, overloaded database objects are now matched using both their ordinary object name and overloaded name, so functions or procedures shown or omitted in filtered navigator-style views may differ.
accepted_impacts.llm_uncertainty: The supplied context does not identify the exact UI views that invoke this loader or define how the two-argument filter interprets overloaded names.
accepted_impacts.behavior_label: Filtered database tree results for overloaded objects

pr_semantic_analysis.change_summary: Object filtering now supports evaluating multiple names for one database object. During navigator tree loading, overloaded objects are filtered using both their ordinary object name and overloaded name; inclusion succeeds when either name matches, while exclusion rejects the object when either name matches.

behavior_changes.description: When tree items are filtered, an overloaded database object is now evaluated under both its normal name and its overloaded name. It remains visible only if the resulting multi-name filter evaluation accepts it; non-overloaded objects continue to be evaluated by their normal name alone.
evidence: The tree-loading path passes two names for DBPOverloadedObject instances and one name for other child items.
The filter helper tests each pattern against any supplied name.

behavior_changes.description: The filter contract now accepts multiple candidate names. An inclusion pattern may match any supplied name, but an exclusion pattern matching any supplied name rejects the candidate.
evidence: The public matching method changed from a single name to a variable-length name list.
Both inclusion and exclusion checks use the same any-name matching helper.

important_symbols.reason: This is the changed consumption point that decides which loaded database objects survive navigator filtering and introduces the overloaded-object-specific behavior.
This public method's contract and matching semantics changed from one candidate name to multiple names, potentially affecting callers beyond the shown tree-loading path.
This helper defines the new any-name behavior shared by inclusion and exclusion processing.

investigation_hints.description: Find every caller of DBSObjectFilter.matches and determine whether any callers rely on its former single-String binary signature or will begin supplying multiple aliases.
Trace which navigator-loading flows produce DBPOverloadedObject children and what overloaded names represent for each database implementation.
Check the intended precedence when inclusion matches one name but exclusion matches another, and whether overloaded names are guaranteed to be non-null.

local_risks.description: The changed public Java signature is source-compatible for ordinary recompiled one-name calls but not binary-compatible with code already linked to matches(String). If separately compiled plugins or modules consume this method, they could fail at linkage until rebuilt.

If an overloaded name can be null, the new second-name path can pass null into pattern matching without a visible guard; regex matching then dereferences that name and could abort filtering rather than merely rejecting the object.

Include and exclude patterns independently inspect every supplied name. Consequently, an object included through one name can still be rejected because another name matches an exclusion; reviewers should confirm that this cross-name precedence is the intended filtering invariant.

uncertainties: The supplied context does not identify all callers of the public matches method or establish whether any caller other than the shown navigator-loading path supplies multiple names.

The observable effect depends on a non-null filter being active and the loaded child being a DBPOverloadedObject; the supplied diff does not establish how often those conditions occur in real installations.
The contract of DBPOverloadedObject.getOverloadedName, including whether it can return null and how it differs from the ordinary object name, is not shown.
It is not established whether DBSObjectFilter is consumed by separately compiled plugins or other binary clients for which the method descriptor change would be compatibility-sensitive.
